one_liner: Rust no_std perfect-hash immutable Map/Set (up to 65,535 keys) with 1.9x-16.9x lower query time than phf.
what_it_does: lute builds immutable minimal-perfect-hash maps and sets over a fixed collection of at most 65,535 keys. The same table can be built at runtime with From/FromIterator (default `construct` feature), at compile time into a `static`/`const` with the `map!`/`set!` proc macros (`macros` feature), or in build.rs with `Map::to_tokens()` (`codegen` feature). Queries use std-style `get`, `get_entry`, `contains_key` and `Index` with `Borrow<Q>` lookups, and keys use the standard `Hash + Eq` traits rather than phf's `PhfHash`. It fills the same role as phf/phf_codegen but has its own types and macros, so switching means rewriting table declarations, not just changing an import.
how_it_is_fast: In the benchmarked 0.1.x release, each query hashes the key once with foldhash, a fast non-cryptographic hasher, where phf_shared uses 128-bit SipHash-1-3. One-entry maps use a linear scan. Maps of up to 10 keys use a 'direct' single-seed perfect hash that needs one multiply-shift (fastrange) and no displacement table. Larger maps use CHD (compress-hash-displace) with a (u16, u16) displacement pair per ~4 keys and a division-free 'fastmod' reduction with a precomputed multiplier, where phf uses `%`. The unreleased main branch replaces this with a PTHash/PtrHash-style scheme: a 16-bit pilot per bucket of ~3 keys, power-of-two bucket selection by shift, and ~1% slack slots remapped back. For n<=12 it uses a 'packed' 16-slot table indexed by one bit window of the hash. Every lookup ends in exactly one key comparison, so a miss costs about the same as a hit.
when_to_use: Read-only lookup tables known ahead of time (keywords, opcode/MIME/unit tables, u64 ID sets) where you use phf today and query latency matters: the author's plots show lute faster than phf at every plotted size from 1 to 65,535 keys.
Tiny tables of about 2-10 keys, where the gap is widest (up to ~16.9x lower amortized time per u64 query on the M1 Pro) because the lookup skips the displacement table entirely.
Miss-heavy membership tests such as 'is this token reserved?': a miss costs one hash plus one comparison, and lute beat phf on all-miss streams as well as all-hit streams.
no_std (+alloc) targets that need a table in a `static` or `const`, built by a proc macro or build.rs with no runtime construction cost.

Keys that are tuples, arrays, ranges, chars, byte strings or C strings (all accepted as literals by map!/set!), or any `Hash + Eq` type when the map is built at runtime or emitted from build.rs with a databake `Bake` impl.
when_not_to_use: More than 65,535 entries: this is a hard limit (u16 indices). Runtime construction panics and the macros emit a compile error.

Build-time or startup construction speed is the priority. PHF search is not reliably faster than phf: about 0.5x-0.8x of phf's speed for short strings at n=128-16,384 on the 9950X, and ~120x slower for long strings at n=9 (~44.9 us vs ~0.37 us). The 0.1.x 'direct' strategy for n<=10 tries up to 65,536 seeds and rehashes every key on each try.

Cross-compiled tables whose keys contain usize/isize, arrays/slices, byte strings, C strings or multibyte-integer arrays, because their hashes depend on pointer width or endianness. map!/set! add a const assertion that fails the build, but build.rs codegen output (bake.rs) has no such guard, so a mismatched target silently returns None for present keys.
You need insertion, mutation, or ordered/sorted iteration: maps are immutable and iteration order is unspecified.
You need proven maturity: one author, 4 stars, 39 crates.io downloads, no independent reproduction, and the main branch has an unreleased algorithm rewrite whose performance has no published plots.

integration.dependencies: foldhash (always); rand_core + rand_xoshiro with the default `construct` feature (0.1.x also pulls hashbrown for duplicate detection); databake + proc-macro-crate with `codegen`; the lute_macros proc-macro crate (syn, quote, proc-macro2, proc-macro-crate) with `macros`
integration.platforms: any Rust target; no_std but requires alloc; no SIMD or architecture-specific code in lute_core
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Maps are immutable after construction, and the benchmark harness requires `Map<K, usize>: Sync` (satisfied for u64 and String keys), so concurrent reads work when K and V are Sync.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same role and similar get/contains_key/Index API, but different types and macros (lute::Map, map!/set!, Map::to_tokens in build.rs), keys use std Hash + Eq instead of phf's PhfHash, and declarations must be rewritten.

gotchas: map!/set! accept only literal-shaped keys. Integer keys need a type suffix (`2u32`, not `2`), and floats, named constants, enum variants and custom structs are rejected. Use build.rs codegen for those.

Runtime construction (From/FromIterator) panics instead of returning a Result. It panics on duplicate keys, on more than 65,535 entries, or when no perfect hash is found within 256 seeds (for example when `Hash` is inconsistent with `Eq`).

Generated tables are not stable across breaking versions. The main branch already changed `from_baked_parts` from displacement pairs to a pilots/packed `BakedStrategy`, so regenerate any generated code you committed after upgrading.

The main-branch lookup uses unsafe `get_unchecked` for pilot, remap and entry indexing and relies on const-time validation in `from_baked_parts`. The released 0.1.1 lookup uses bounds-checked indexing.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Compared with QuickPHF (README: about 2x phf on lookups and more than 10x faster construction), pick lute when per-query latency matters more than table-generation time, or when you want runtime, proc-macro and build.rs construction from one API with tuple/array/range literal keys. Pick QuickPHF when fast build-time generation matters. Pick hashify for pure string-keyed `match` replacement. There are no head-to-head numbers between lute and either sibling.
verified_claims_summary: The author ran divan benchmarks on an Apple M1 Pro and an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X (rustc version and flags not stated), comparing lute 0.1.x with phf 0.14 maps assembled at runtime from phf_generator output. Keys were u64, short strings and 78-byte shared-prefix strings at n=1-65,535. Values read from the SVG plots show median isolated lookups 1.9x-9.8x faster than phf and amortized per-query time 1.9x-16.9x faster at every plotted point (e.g. u64 n=2048 hit ~1.73 ns vs ~8.04 ns on the 9950X), while PHF search time ranges from ~10x faster to ~120x slower. The plotted code replays queries in key-generation order (shuffling was added later), and the plots predate the main branch's pilot/packed rewrite.
status_note: Active single-author project (last commit 2026-08-18; 0.1.1 on crates.io since 2026-06-22; no issues filed). It is MIT OR Apache-2.0 and a small pure-Rust workspace that is easy to vendor, but main holds an unreleased algorithm rewrite, so pin 0.1.1 unless you have re-benchmarked HEAD.
